name: Sivalokanathar Temple, Gramam (Thirumundeeswaram)
deity: Shiva as Sivalokanathar (Mundeeswarar), with the Goddess Soundaryanayaki
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu, sung by Appar (7th century); rebuilt in stone in the 10th century under the Cholas
summary: At Gramam — the Thirumundeeswaram of Appar's hymn — Shiva is the Lord of Shiva's own world, in a village temple that the Chola prince Rajaditya's men raised in stone more than a thousand years ago.

sections.history: Gramam is a village near Thiruvennainallur, south-west of Villupuram, and its temple to Shiva as Sivalokanathar is the Thirumundeeswaram of the Tevaram. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of the shrines of Nadu Nadu; Appar sang its Lord in a Thiruthandagam pathigam preserved in the sixth Tirumurai. In the tenth century the village, then called Mouli-gramam, was the headquarters of Rajaditya, the warrior son of the Chola king Parantaka I, and inscriptions record that the shrine was rebuilt in stone in his time, around 943 CE, with gifts of lamps for its worship. The present masonry owes much to Vijayanagara-period rebuilding in the sixteenth century, and the temple is administered today by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
sections.architecture: The temple is a compact Dravidian shrine of the Nadu Nadu countryside, with the lingam of Sivalokanathar in the sanctum and a separate shrine for the Goddess Soundaryanayaki. Its walls carry the Chola inscriptions that tell the story of its stone rebuilding and the lamps endowed for the Lord — among the more valuable records of Rajaditya's years in this region — while the later halls and enclosure reflect the Vijayanagara renewal.
sections.legends: Tradition gives the temple its old name: Thindi and Mundi, the gatekeepers of Shiva's own abode, came down to earth and worshipped the Lord here, and so the place was called Thirumundeeswaram, after Mundi. In the shrine they served, Shiva is Sivalokanathar, the Lord of Shiva's world. Appar is remembered here too: tradition counts Gramam among the temples where he carried out his humble service of clearing the temple grounds with his small hoe — the uzhavarappani for which the Tevaram saint is loved.
sections.festivals: Chitra Pournami, the full moon of the month of Chithirai, and the Aani Thirumanjanam, the great ceremonial bathing of the Lord in June–July, are the principal festivals, with Maha Shivaratri and the monthly pradosham; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Gramam is a quiet village temple, and its interest lies in its layered story: a hymn of Appar, a tenth-century prince's stone shrine, and the gatekeepers' legend. Pilgrims often combine it with Thiruvennainallur nearby on the Pennai, where the Lord came as an old man to claim the young Sundarar for his service.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Gramam lies near Thiruvennainallur, about 15 km south-west of Villupuram, and buses stop at Gramam close to the temple. Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction; Puducherry has the closest airport, and Chennai and Tiruchirappalli the nearest major airports.
